lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you met human rights. In which year was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights agreed? (1948.) Today: constitutions, and freedom of speech and its limits.
A constitution is a country's most important set of rules: how its government is made up, what each part may do, the limits on its power, and the rights of the people. Other laws must fit it.

Most countries have a codified constitution, written in one document. The USA's, written in 1787, is one of the oldest still in use; India's, from 1950, is one of the longest. The UK's is uncodified: it is found in many laws, court rulings and customs.

Changing a constitution is made hard on purpose. In the USA an amendment needs two-thirds of both houses of Congress and three-quarters of the states: 38 of 50. The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights of 1791, protect freedoms such as speech.

Freedom of expression is a human right (Article 19 of the Universal Declaration): you may say what you think, share ideas and disagree with leaders, even when others dislike your views. It protects criticising the government and peaceful protest.

But it has limits, to protect other people: threats, stirring up hatred against a group, lies that harm someone's good name (defamation), and sharing people's private information are not protected. Countries draw these lines a little differently.

Online, the same laws apply, and websites add their own rules. Rights come with responsibilities: to respect other people's rights. In the UK, the Human Rights Act 1998 put the European Convention on Human Rights, from grade 6, into UK law.

Try it in the world: write a constitution for your server: how leaders are chosen, what they may and may not do, and three rights every player has. Decide how hard it should be to change. Next: active citizens.

exercises.explain: A country's most important set of rules about its government and people's rights.

exercises.prompt: The UK's constitution is written in one single document.
exercises.hint: Where is the UK's constitution found?
exercises.explain: False: it is uncodified, spread across laws, court rulings and customs.

exercises.prompt: Which is protected by freedom of expression?
exercises.hint: Which one harms nobody else's safety or rights?
exercises.explain: Criticising the government; the others harm other people and are not protected.

exercises.prompt: Which article of the Universal Declaration protects freedom of expression?
exercises.hint: It is in the second half of the 30 articles.
exercises.explain: Article 19 protects freedom of expression: to say what you think and share ideas.

exercises.prompt: When was the USA's constitution written?
exercises.explain: 1787: the USA's constitution is one of the oldest still in use.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: protected as free speech, or not?
items: saying a new law is unfair
writing that a film was boring
stirring up hatred against a group
exercises.hint: Free speech protects opinions, even unpopular ones, but not harm to others.
exercises.explain: Free speech: unfair law, boring film, peaceful protest. Not protected: threats, hatred, private photos.

exercises.prompt: A US amendment needs three-quarters of the 50 states. How many states is that, going up to a whole state?
exercises.hint: Find three-quarters of 50, then go up to the next whole number.

exercises.prompt: Why is changing a constitution made hard?
exercises.hint: What if a new government could change the rules every week?
choices: so it is not changed on a whim
exercises.explain: So the country's basic rules and rights are not changed quickly or carelessly.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: lies that harm a good name
exercises.hint: One is about how it is written, one changes it, one is a harm, one is a list.
exercises.explain: Codified: one document. Amendment: a change. Defamation: harmful lies. Bill of Rights: the first ten amendments.

exercises.prompt: Free speech protects views that many people dislike.
exercises.hint: Would free speech mean much if it only covered popular views?
exercises.explain: True: it protects unpopular opinions, as long as they do not threaten or harm others.

exercises.prompt: Zara posts that a classmate stole something, but it is not true. What is that?
exercises.hint: Is it true, and does it harm someone's good name?
exercises.explain: Defamation: a false claim that harms a person's good name, which free speech does not protect.

exercises.prompt: Why does free speech have limits?
choices: to protect other people's safety and rights
exercises.explain: Limits protect other people from threats, hatred and harmful lies, while opinions stay free.

exercises.prompt: The US Bill of Rights came in 1791, and the Universal Declaration in 1948. How many years apart?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.

exercises.prompt: Online, anything goes: the law does not apply.
exercises.hint: Do threats become harmless on a screen?
exercises.explain: False: the same laws apply online, and websites add their own rules.

exercises.prompt: Who must follow a country's constitution?
exercises.hint: Think of the rule of law from grade 6.
exercises.explain: Everyone, leaders included: that is the rule of law.

exercises.prompt: The US Senate has 100 members. An amendment needs two-thirds of them, if all vote. How many senators is that, going up to a whole senator?
exercises.hint: Find two-thirds of 100. You cannot have part of a senator.
exercises.explain: 100 × 2 ÷ 3 is about 66.7. 66 senators would be just under two-thirds, so 67 are needed. Then the change still needs three-quarters of the states.
